question: When two power-driven vessels are approaching each other head-on, what action should each operator take?
choice_a: The larger vessel should always reverse
choice_b: Each vessel should alter course to starboard (right) so that they pass port-to-port, like cars on a road
choice_c: Both vessels should stop dead in the water and wait for instructions
choice_d: Each vessel should turn to port (left) so they pass starboard-to-starboard
explanation: In a head-on meeting situation, the Navigation Rules direct both power-driven vessels to alter course to starboard, passing each other port side to port side, similar to traffic keeping to the right.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland) head-on meeting situation (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel is the 'give-way' vessel that must take early and substantial action to avoid a collision?
choice_c: The vessel that has the other vessel approaching on its own starboard (right) side
choice_d: The vessel that has the other vessel approaching on its own port (left) side
explanation: When two power-driven vessels are crossing, the vessel that sees the other vessel on its own starboard side is the give-way vessel and must take early, obvious action, usually by slowing, stopping, or altering course to avoid crossing ahead of the other vessel.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules crossing-situation right-of-way (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: In a crossing situation, what is the 'stand-on' vessel generally required to do?
choice_a: Immediately speed up to cross ahead of the other vessel
choice_b: Turn hard to port regardless of the situation
choice_c: Sound five short blasts and continue without any other precaution
choice_d: Maintain its current course and speed so the give-way vessel can predict its movement, while remaining ready to take action if a collision becomes imminent
explanation: The stand-on vessel should hold its course and speed to remain predictable, but the rules still require it to take avoiding action if the give-way vessel fails to act and a collision risk develops.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules crossing-situation right-of-way (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: When one vessel is overtaking another, which vessel has the right-of-way?
choice_a: The vessel being overtaken (the 'stand-on' vessel) always has the right-of-way over the vessel attempting to pass
choice_b: The overtaking vessel always has the right-of-way
choice_c: Whichever vessel signals first has the right-of-way
choice_d: Right-of-way in an overtaking situation is determined by vessel size alone
explanation: In an overtaking situation, the vessel being passed keeps its course and speed as the stand-on vessel, while the overtaking vessel is the give-way vessel and must keep clear until safely past.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules overtaking-situation right-of-way (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: Under the Navigation Rules, how is a vessel considered to be 'overtaking' another vessel?
choice_a: Any vessel traveling faster than another is automatically overtaking, regardless of angle
choice_b: It is approaching the other vessel from more than 22.5 degrees abaft (behind) the other vessel's beam
choice_c: It is approaching from directly ahead of the other vessel
choice_d: It is approaching from either side at a 90-degree angle
explanation: A vessel is deemed to be overtaking when it approaches another vessel from a direction more than 22.5 degrees abaft that vessel's beam, meaning it is coming up mostly from behind rather than crossing or meeting head-on.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules overtaking definition (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: In general, which type of vessel must give way to a sailing vessel under sail alone, when both are power-driven versus wind-driven?
choice_a: Right-of-way between sail and power vessels is determined only by which vessel is larger
choice_b: Sailing vessels have no right-of-way status under the Navigation Rules
choice_c: A power-driven vessel must generally give way to a sailing vessel under sail alone
choice_d: A sailing vessel must always give way to a power-driven vessel
explanation: Under the general right-of-way hierarchy, a power-driven vessel must generally keep out of the way of a sailing vessel under sail alone, since sailing vessels have less maneuverability relative to the wind.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules right-of-way hierarchy between power-driven and sailing vessels (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: On Maryland's tidal Chesapeake Bay, why must recreational vessels give way to large commercial ships operating in the marked shipping channels?
choice_a: Commercial ships always have lower right-of-way status than recreational boats under the Navigation Rules
choice_b: Recreational boats are legally forbidden from ever being near a shipping channel
choice_c: Commercial vessels are required to always stop for recreational boaters
choice_d: Large ships are constrained by their draft to the marked channel and cannot maneuver or stop quickly, making them 'vessels constrained by their draft' or otherwise limited in their ability to maneuver
explanation: Deep-draft commercial ships transiting the Chesapeake Bay's dredged shipping channels often cannot leave the channel without running aground, and they require enormous distances to slow or stop, so recreational boaters are expected to stay clear and give way well in advance.
source_note: Chesapeake Bay commercial shipping traffic navigation guidance (Maryland DNR/NRP boating safety messaging), combined with universal Navigation Rules provisions on vessels constrained by draft

question: What sound signal does a power-driven vessel give to indicate it intends to alter course to starboard (in a meeting or crossing situation, under the Inland Navigation Rules)?
explanation: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, one short blast signals an intent to alter course to starboard (or to pass on the other vessel's port side), two short blasts signals an intent to turn to port, and three short blasts indicates operating astern propulsion.
source_note: Universal Inland Navigation Rules maneuvering and warning signals (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: What does a signal of five or more short, rapid blasts of a horn mean under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: A request for the other vessel to increase speed
choice_b: A danger or doubt signal, warning that the other vessel's intentions or actions are not understood or that a collision risk exists
choice_c: A greeting exchanged between two friendly vessels
choice_d: A signal that a vessel is about to anchor
explanation: Five or more short, rapid blasts is the danger or doubt signal, used when a vessel does not understand another's intentions or actions, or believes insufficient action is being taken to avoid a collision.
source_note: Universal Inland Navigation Rules danger/doubt signal (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: In restricted visibility, such as fog on the Chesapeake Bay, what should an operator do in addition to sounding the required fog signals?
choice_a: Turn off all navigation lights to save power
choice_b: Stop sounding any signals since visibility is already reduced
choice_c: Reduce speed to a safe speed for the conditions and post an extra lookout, using radar if available
choice_d: Increase speed to clear the area of low visibility as quickly as possible
explanation: In fog or other restricted visibility, boaters must proceed at a safe speed for the conditions, keep a proper lookout by sight and hearing, and use any available means such as radar, in addition to sounding the required fog signals.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules conduct in restricted visibility (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: Which vessels are generally given the least maneuverability and therefore the highest right-of-way priority under the Navigation Rules' general hierarchy?
choice_a: Personal watercraft, because of their small size
choice_c: Anchored recreational vessels, which always outrank every other category
choice_d: Vessels not under command and vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver, such as a vessel laying cable or one disabled by mechanical failure
explanation: The Navigation Rules' right-of-way hierarchy places vessels not under command (unable to maneuver, such as due to mechanical breakdown) and vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver (such as those engaged in dredging or towing) near the top, since they have the least ability to avoid other traffic.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules general right-of-way hierarchy (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: Why should a small recreational vessel avoid crossing close in front of a large commercial vessel or tug-and-barge combination on the Bay?
choice_a: Large vessels have significant blind spots close to the bow and need long distances to stop or turn, making a close crossing extremely dangerous
choice_b: It is always legal and safe as long as the small boat is faster
choice_c: Large vessels are required to always yield regardless of position
choice_d: Commercial vessels cannot see recreational boats at any distance
explanation: Large ships and tug-and-barge tows have substantial blind zones near the bow and require a long distance to slow, stop, or turn, so crossing closely in front of one is highly dangerous even though the smaller vessel may appear to have more room to maneuver.
source_note: Chesapeake Bay commercial shipping traffic hazard guidance (Maryland DNR/NRP boating safety messaging), combined with universal large-vessel maneuverability fundamentals

question: What does it mean for a vessel to maintain a 'proper lookout' as required by the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: Watching only for buoys and ignoring other vessels
choice_b: Using sight, hearing, and all other available means to be continuously aware of other vessels, obstructions, and conditions that could create a risk of collision
choice_c: Checking behind the boat only once at the start of a trip
choice_d: Relying solely on other vessels to avoid a collision
explanation: The Navigation Rules require every vessel to maintain a proper lookout by sight and hearing, as well as by all available means appropriate to the circumstances, to fully assess the risk of collision at all times.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules proper-lookout requirement (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: What is meant by operating at a 'safe speed' under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: A fixed speed of exactly 5 mph on all waters
choice_b: Whatever speed keeps the vessel on plane, regardless of traffic or visibility
choice_c: A speed that allows a vessel to take proper and effective action to avoid a collision and to stop within a distance appropriate to the prevailing circumstances and conditions
choice_d: The fastest speed the vessel's engine can achieve
explanation: Safe speed depends on factors like visibility, traffic density, maneuverability, background lighting, and sea/wind conditions, and it requires being able to stop or take avoiding action in time given those conditions.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules safe-speed requirement (NASBLA-aligned course content)

question: How should a recreational vessel operator navigate near dredging operations or work vessels commonly seen maintaining Maryland's shipping channels?
choice_a: Pass as closely as possible to save time
choice_b: Ignore the work vessel since it has no special right-of-way status
choice_c: Increase speed to create a wake that pushes the work vessel out of the way
choice_d: Slow down, keep a safe distance, and give way, since dredges and work vessels are often restricted in their ability to maneuver and may have equipment or lines extending into the water
explanation: Dredges and other work vessels maintaining Maryland's channels are frequently restricted in their ability to maneuver and may have anchors, cables, or pipelines extending underwater, so boaters should slow down, keep well clear, and give way.
source_note: Chesapeake Bay channel maintenance/dredging vessel hazard guidance, combined with universal Navigation Rules provisions on vessels restricted in ability to maneuver
